speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Last evening when the committee rose we had passed the first item.
Fort St. John building for telegraph service, $4,000.
Does the construction of this building indicate an extension of the line from Fort St. John to Finlay Forks.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. C. ELLIOTT (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
No, it does not indicate that. It is to provide for the construction of a building for the telegraph service at Fort St. John, as requested on several occasions within the past year by Mr. J. E. Gobeil, general superintendent of telegraphs, and by District Super-

intendent Noel. The telegraph office is at present located in rented premises, the owner of which requires them and wishes to obtain possession as early as posible during the coming summer. There are no other quarters obtainable and consequently the only alternative is to erect the proposed building at an estimated cost of 84,000.

For the last two years a request has been before the minister for the extension of that line from Fort St. John to the head of the Peace River canyon, a distance of about fifteen miles. That is a very necessary piece of telegraph line. Could the minister indicate whether he has any idea of giving it serious consideration in his supplementary estimates?
As to what may appear in the supplementary estimates, it is difficult to say. The matter is under consideration. It has been pressed more especially during the last year.
Can the minister say he has given it favourable consideration so far?
I cannot say that with regard to any item, but it will be considered.

Item agreed to.
Telephone line from Dawson Creek to Sunset Prairie, $2,000.

Will this complete the
line?
Yes.
How much was spent on the line last summer?

Item agreed to.
Telephone line from Rolla to Rolla Landing, $1,400.
Is this to complete, and how much was spent on the fine last year?
The expenditure last year was $233.

That is a pretty small
amount.
We hope to do better this year.
T should hope so. Is it proposed to finish it this year?
Yes.

Item agreed to.

Supply-Public Works-Telegraph Lines
Telephone line from Lillooet to Squamish, $23,250.

I understand that this is
a new line. Would the minister give the details?

Perhaps I might speak to this item as it happens to be in a district with which I am very familiar. The line is an extension from Lillooet to Squamish. That country has been opened u,p for some fifteen years and communities have been established along the railway line. The railway company, the Pacific Great Eastern, have been somewhat embarrassed by all the demands made on their system, and they have particularly requested to be relieved from the responsibility of providing a public service. They are so much concerned about the situation that they offered the use of their telegraph poles. The result is that a proposal has been made to the government that they should provide the wire in this district, which must necessarily become an integral part of the Dominion telegraph andi telephone system, and take over the service. I am quite sure the government will find that the service will be remunerative from the start. The matter has been before the government for many years, and I want to commend the minister for bringing down this vote, which will give to these communities extending over a distance of eighty or ninety miles the service which they have long sought.

There is only a very small office to accommodate the present staff at Lillooet. Necessarily, if you are going to build a new line, the work of the staff will be increased and additions to the staff will probably be necessary. Has the minister received any report from his officers as to the necessity for a new building in Lillooet to accommodate the additional staff necessary in connection with this extension ?

We have had a request
of that kind, and it is receiving consideration.

My question was, has a
report been made to the minister by his officials as to the necessity of a new public building there?
Yes.

That report is before the
minister?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Yukon telegraph system-general repairs and improvements, $20,100.

What part of the Yukon
does this vote cover?
This is for the Yukon main line from Ashcroft to Dawson.
The minister informed me last night that the first item covered that line.
The item we were speaking of last night was for the northern part of British Columbia up to the Skeena.

But the minister said that
it was part of the Yukon system.
Yes.
What part? From Ashcroft to Dawson is the whole system, and apparently', it is divided into two divisions.
This is the Yukon division, and the one we were speaking of last night is the British Columbia division.

I do not quite understand
the minister, because it is the same line. The whole sy'stem extends from Ashcroft to Dawson, and apparently you have two divisions. Where is the dividing point between the two divisions?

The first division is the
one that we were speaking of. last night, from Ashcroft to Hazelton, and the other is from Hazelton to Dawson.
What further extensions of telephonic communication has the department undertaken in northern British Columbia since 1928?

My information is that
there are two small branches. I shall be very glad to furnish my hon. friend with the particulars.

From Fraser lake? The
government has done some very good work there. I would like to know what further work has been done in the past year in extending telephone communication in northern British Columbia.

There were repairs and
reconstruction in that district last year, but no new lines.

Are any new lines under
contemplation for the present year?

None except what has
been mentioned.

Except what I asked the
minister about last night?
Yes.

Has the minister received
a request for extension of lines in this district during the coming year?
,6	COMMONS
Supply-Public Works-Telegraph Lines

From a territory such as
that, there are always requests. There have been requests this year. I have not a list of them here, but I shall be pleased to furnish it to my hon. friend if he wishes it. Of course, he will understand that I have before me only the details of such items as are in the estimates.

I would point out that since 1925 there has been before the Department of Public Works a request for the construction of a line from the One Hundred Mile House to Green lake. There is a complete report in the department on that proposed line, and I should like to impress upon the minister the necessity of giving that section of the country telephone communication. It is an isolated section, with quite a number of people in it, and I am quite sure that if the minister were only aware of the conditions he would not hesitate a minute to extend the service into that district. The people are from fifteen to twenty miles from the main line of travel, a long way from doctors, and so forth. They are entirely cut off from communication with the outside world except by road. I believe for two or three years the department refused to consider the requests because there were no permanent roads in that section. The provincial government has now completed the roads, and I think it is up to the minister to give serious consideration to the request. They have been asking for the service for a number of years, and I think they are entitled to it. I should be very pleased indeed if the minister would bear this in mind and give it his special consideration.

I should like to know why this policy of the government building telephone lines in remote districts is confined to British Columbia. Many outlying districts in different parts of Saskatchewan are without telephone communication, and we have to build connecting lines ourselves or get the provincial government to do so. Why should the federal government build telephone lines in the outlying districts of British Columbia; what is the policy of the government in that regard?

The distinction between
British Columbia and Saskatchewan is that Saskatchewan has a government telephone system and British Columbia at the present time has a privately owned system. The policy of the government in regard to the lines to which we have been referring is, as soon as it is at all practicable from the fi-
TMr. Fraser.]
nancial standpoint, to provide these settlers, who are largely pioneers, with reasonable facilities for keeping in touch with the more settled portions of the country and with civilization generally.

Is it the intention of the
government to hand over its present telephone lines in the province to the British Columbia Telephone Company? I find that from Kamloops right through to Vanderhoof that company is taking over the government lines. I believe the federal government, realizing the importance of opening up the country, take a larger view of the situation than would a private corporation. What is the policy of the government in this regard? Are they ready to hand over to the British Columbia Telephone Company all their lines and leave the company to continue the development of necessary extension lines through northern British Columbia.
The policy of the government is to sell our lines to the company when we are able to get from them a reasonable offer. As my hon. friend very well knows, these are pioneer lines to a large extent.
Yes.

These lines are liabilities to a very great extent so long as they remain in our hands, and as soon as W'e can get commercial concerns to take them over at anything like an equitable price we are glad to transfer them.

Before doing so, surely you
will admit the desirability of laying down certain conditions to be carried out by the company regarding further development of the system. Do you have a definite understanding before you hand over your telephone communications to a private company that that company will continue the development in these very important areas where hundreds of people expect telephone communication?

That is the policy. My
hon. friend will understand that in selling one of these lines to which additions will have to be made in the future it is very difficult to get the purchasing company to agree to undertake all the extensions that might be required within a period of say, five or ten years. We do not go so far as that. We do provide, however, that they shall take care of all the subscribers who are receiving service at the time the line is handed over. We look after future subscribers either by making extensions to the line or by some other arrangement as the necessity arises.

Supply-Public Works-Telegraph Lines
We discussed this matter last session, Mr. Chairman, and I do not think the minister went as far then as he does now. All I can say is, I think the policy a rotten one.
Is that parliamentary?

We go into unsettled country and at large expense build a telephone line that is badly needed by the settlers, and the operation of the line shows an annual deficit for which the minister is more or less blamed. Then when the line begins to return a little profit we transfer it to a private company.
I know that when that has been done in the past an effort has been made to stipulate that the same rates and conditions shall prevail, but, as the minister has admitted, you cannot bind the company as to its future policy. Then we have the question of further extensions cropping up. We turn over the main line because it is profitable, keeping such portions as are unprofitable and operating them at the expense of the government. A little side line, for instance, is needed, and as it connects with the line of the private company we go there for service. Then you find, as I have found, what their ideas are about building a branch line. In the particular case to which I am referring I wanted a side line extension of a few hundred yards. It was a perfectly reasonable request. I was told I would have to build the whole line at my expense, and it would then become the property of the company. Well, the day it was finished the company put another couple of people on the line. That is a small illustration of the policy of these private companies. I do not think it is fair to the public or to the government to carry out such a policy. When we come down here, as I said before, we find all the government lines showing a deficit, and we blame the minister or his officials, but it is because we have turned over to private companies the profitable ones. I do not think that a good policy; I said so last year, and I feel so still.

I had the privilege last
session of saying a word of appreciation of the government telegraph service in our province. We seldom hear anything in the house about the service. It is strictly a pioneer service, and I for one would regret indeed to see the system curtailed or disintegrated. I should like very much, as the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) has said, to see the government continue the work they have so long carried on in connection with this telegraph service. I am sure hon. members from the prairies do not fully appreciate
some of these far-flung districts in British Columbia which the government telegraph service is connecting up with civilization. Many of these districts would be without direct communication to-day but for the government service. On a commercial basis it would be absolutely impossible to maintain the present service. True, there may be some deficit annually, but I believe that that deficit will not be lessened by selling such sections of the system as a private corporation might feel disposed to take over. I rather think the government will find on careful investigation that those sections are remunerative and help, in part, to cany the burden of the whole system. This is a pioneer service which is due to the remote settlements in our province, and which I believe the government and the government alone can supply.
Is any revenue derived by the government from these lines?

The revenue derived last year by the government from lines operated by it was somewhere in the vicinity of $298,000. When my hon. friends speak of revenue from these lines I think they must bear in mind that the cost always exceeds the revenue. These lines serve pioneer districts, and I regret my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has not a better idea of what the government is doing. At least I regret that he is not able to express his idea in more flattering terms than he saw fit to do in regard to the action of the government in this connection. When he used the expression that the government builds these lines, operates them for a certain length of time and turns over the more profitable parts to private companies, he is not as accurate as is his usual custom in statements before the house. The government is not turning over the more profitable portions but it is turning over the less unprofitable ones. Those are the only parts which a commercial company will take over. The government is very anxious to give aid to the people handicapped in the way the pioneers are handicapped; we appreciate that they go into these isolated districts and we wish to give them the best service we can as long as there is a return reasonably commensurate with the service given.

It would be interesting to the house to know that the Yukon system forms part of the old Collins overland system which was to extend from San Francisco to the Aleutian islands, thence into Russia and back to London. That was put out of operation in 1865 when the Atlantic cable was successfully constructed. As a matter of fact
1478	COMMONS
Supply-Public Works-Telegraph Lines
in 1S65 this line was built as far as Hazelton, and it has been used for the Cariboo country ever since. It was operated until the time of confederation by the government or by some local company; at any rate at the time of confederation it was taken over by the federal government. It constituted one of the grants which we made to the federal government when we entered confederation. The federal government turned it over to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and it was operated for quite a number of years by that railway. When the Yukon territory opened up they wanted telegraphic communication. The line at that time only went as far as Quesnel, but in 1898 when the Dawson country opened up and it was necessary to provide it with telegraphic communication the whole line was reconstructed from Ashcroft to Dawson, a distance of 2,000 miles. It is not by any means a local line; it is 2,000 miles in length and the objective in view when the line was built was to put the Yukon, especially Dawson City and Prince Rupert, in telegraphic communication with the outside world. There was no telegraphic system in Prince Rupert at that time, and for a long time it served the northern country. It is impossible for the government to operate at a profit a line of that length which runs through a country so sparsely settled. I wish to say in fairness to the minister and to the government that so far as the system is concerned it has always been of an excellent character; the line is kept in first class condition and provides the very best service to the people of that district. The complaint I make to the minister is not in connection with the main line but in the extension of these facilities to the outlying contiguous sections. In these days settlers expect some conveniences; they are not satisfied as they were twenty years ago to get along without telegraphic and telephonic communication. I can name twenty communities in my own constituency which are asking to be connected with this main trunk line, and the reason offered is that insufficient attention is given to the extension of these lines. The contention is that the main line is so overloaded that it will not carry a greater load. I do not know whether that is so or not, but it does seem to me that if it is overloaded some remedy could be found to give the constituencies throughout that country the telephonic communication to which I think they are entitled. I have twenty or twenty-five requests for extensions, and it seems to me it would be good business for the government to give more consideration than they have been giving in the past to the extension of these lines. We are pleased to get extensions 
from time to time, but let me tell the minister that he is by no means keeping up with the public demand. It seems to me that when you consider how the expenses in connection with all branches of the government have expanded we are not expecting too much and our requests are no more exorbitant than they are in other parts of the Dominion. If the minister would give the same consideration to that part of the country that he does to the matter of wharves and breakwaters in the province of Quebec and the lower parts of the Dominion, he would extend the telegraph service in British Columbia.

I can well appreciate the difficulties of these settlers who have not telephonic communication, and I understand the contention of the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Fraser). On the prairies, however, we do this work ourselves, and I cannot help but think that this is a provincial matter and should be handled by the province of British Columbia.
No, no.

Why should the province not pay for it? We in Saskatchewan have never had help from the Dominion government in this respect, although the territory is very extensive; in British Columbia, however, telephonic communication is furnished without the expenditure of one dollar by the province, and we spend money in other parts of the country for many things which are provincial or municipal in character. It seems to me that this is a matter of a provincial character and should not be charged to the country at large.
I wonder if the minster could tell us how the rates compare with the rates on provincial lines?

There is a regular tariff,
of course, for the use of these lines. With regard to the question raised by the hon. member for Rosetown, this has been the policy in British Columbia for many years, and these lines, as the hon. member for Cariboo says, are old pioneer telegraph lines, which hawe been extended from time to time. It has been suggested that we should extend these lines more rapidly to keep pace with the development of the country, but I would remind the committee that development is taking place in this country so rapidly that we are just doing the best we can with the money placed at our disposal, in an endeavour to keep somewhere in sight of the development which is proceeding. I want to say to him further that I hope the government is sympathetic;

Supply-Public Works-Telegraph Lines
I know the officials of the department are, and I hope the minister is most sympathetic to these pioneers in British Columbia. Some instances	have	come to	the	notice of thedepartment which, were it not for taking up the time of the committee, I should like to recall to show how valuable are these lines to the existence of the settlements they serve. Perhaps I might just refer for a moment to an incident which occurred, I believe within the last year	and a	half, not	far	from Hazelton,to which	point	my hon.	friend has referred.A report	came	in that	the	line north of
Hazelton was grounded, and that they could not get through. An inspector started out at about four o'clock in the morning with a dog team in an endeavour to find out where the break had occurred. When he got about forty miles from Hazelton he found that the wire had been taken off the pole and grounded, clearly by some individual. It was not an accident; it had been done designedly. There had been a fresh snowfall and he could not see any tracks, but he did find a little path through the bush which he followed to an Indian wigwam not far from the point where the line was grounded. He knocked at the door without getting any response. When he opened the door and went in he found an Indian, the lone inhabitant of that district, almost in a dying condition. He had no neighbours and no* means of getting into communication with the outside world; he had enough strength only to crawl over and ground the telegraph wire and crawl back to his shanty. The inspector put him on the sleigh and took him down to the hospital in Hazelton, where it was thought he had but a very slight chance of getting better. However, with the nursing and medical attention he received, in about three weeks he was able to go back to his shanty. Certainly his life was saved as a result of his being able to make this contact with the outside world. Many instances of that kind have come to the notice of the department which show how very useful this service is. However, my hon. friend will understand that if you have a line going north and south, what you might call a trunk line, it is pretty difficult to extend your services, with anything like the same efficiency, by means of branch lines.

In reply to the hon. member for Rosetown, I think it might be advisable to read this little paragraph in order to convince the house that these telegraph lines should be continued for some time yet. It states the case very well:
The Dominion government telegraph service was commenced with the object of furnishing
rapid communication in outlying districts where the amount of business was so small that commercial companies would not enter the field, but -where the public interests required that there should be communication.

From what is my hon.
friend reading?

I am reading from the Canada Year Book in connection with the telegraph systems inaugurated by the Dominion government. I want to urge that you should not doubt for one moment the advisability of continuing the federal telegraph system throughout these vast areas which must depend upon this government. The hon. member for Rosetown said that the prairie provinces maintained provincial telegraph and telephone lines, and he assumed that it would be proper for the province of British Columbia to do the same thing, but I contend that the hon. member has not been informed with regard to the objects of the Dominion telegraph system; he does not understand the situation. We do not desire to make money; we want to develop Canada; we want to place in these vast areas the men and women who in the years to come will bring immense returns for *what we do. You, Mr. Minister, are the agent; you have the power; you have the vision and the foresight. Aik we ask is that you see to it that where there is a settlement or a body of people, you carry out the policy of extending the lines both north and south and east and west. Keep to that policy, and whether or not the present government is defeated, you will have the gratitude of hundreds of these people.

I must congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver North, and myself for having converted the hon. member for Skeena. Ten minutes ago he expressed his satisfaction with the sale of these lines by the government.

Pardonnez-moi, which I
think is good French; I asked whether or not there was any danger to the development of the country and the safeguarding of the people through handing over these lines to a private company. That was the question; I think the minister will corroborate that statement.
But before that you made the statement that you would be satisfied.

Let us get some items
through.

The minister has related an instance in which the telegraph line was the means of saving the life of an Indian inhabitant of that part of the country. The reason we are asking for the extension of these
1480	_	COMMONS
Supply-Public Works-Telegraph Lines
lines is, in many eases, to save the lives of the people who may desire to locate 25, 30 or 50 miles from the main line. Now I am going to relate an incident which will illustrate what the minister is doing when he refuses to give that service; and by the way this happened at a point called Green lake, for which I have been asking this line since 1025. This is a cattle country, with considerable timber. As a young man was riding after cattle, pushing his horse pretty fast, as is the custom, the horse passed too close to a tree and the man's knee was caught between the side of the horse and the tree. His leg was wrenched and the femur was broken off short at the hip bone. He was unable to get out of his saddle but he knew that his neighbour's children were chasing cattle nearby. He rode over and found the two girls, one fifteen and the other sixteen years of age, and told them his condition. They were unable to lift him out of the saddle, but they led the horse to a tree, threw a rope over a limib and hoisted him out of the saddle. Having done that, the girls rode twentydive miles to the telephone office to get in touch with a doctor. The girls made him as comfortable as they could, but he was forced to remain in that condition for twelve hours before the doctor arrived to take him to the nearest hospital, to reach which he was forced to travel a distance of 125 miles. Imagine a man in that condition, having to pay for the conveyance of himself to the hospital, having to pay the doctor to come and see him, and then having to remain in the hospital for five or six weeks. We want to extend the telephonic communication to these people so that they will be able to take care of just such emergencies as that. The post office itself was made out of some private rooms and forms part of an old dwelling house. The remaining portion of the building is a private dwelling. is taken up by desks, stove, safe, stamp tables and desk, boxes and wicket ledges.
